Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM2101 : Cell and Molecular Biology { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1 Introduction to Cell Biology (3 hours)
Discovery and history of cell biology, Cell theory and modern concepts, Eukaryotic vs. Prokaryotic cell, structure and function of cellular components
Module 2 Gene expression and regulation (10 hours)
Central dogma, replication, transcription, translation, operon model

Membrane structure and function, types of membrane transport

Students will be able to-

2) Understand different steps in the central dogma of molecular biology, enzymes involved in synthesis of DNA, RNA and protein.
3) Explain the nature of signals, sorting, SRP Receptor in the targeting of proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum and chaperone mediated protein folding.

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE6232 : Advanced Reinforced Concrete Design { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1: [6 hrs]
Deflection of reinforced concrete beams: Short-term and long-term deflection, calculation of deflection by IS 456.
Estimation of crack width in reinforced concrete members: Factor affecting crack width, calculation of crack width.
Module 2: [6 hrs]
Design of concrete corbels: Load transfer, initial dimensioning, analysis and design of corbels.
Design of Deep Beams: Behaviour of deep beams, Flexural bending stresses and shear stresses, design of deep beams
Module 3: [8 hrs]
Seismic analysis of reinforced concrete buildings: basic seismology and characteristics of ground motions, Different methods of computing earthquake forces on buildings.

Seismic design of reinforced concrete buildings: Different methods of computing earthquake forces on buildings, Ductility considerations in earthquake resistant design of RC buildings, Earthquake resistant design of multistorey RC building based on IS 13920.

Evaluation of wind loads on RC buildings.
Design of shear walls: Classification of shear walls, Loads in shear walls, design of rectangular and flanged shear walls.

1 .

Students will learn the analysis of reinforced concrete buildings under seismic and wind loadings.
2 .

Students will learn to compute the deflection and crack width of RC beams.
3 .

Students will learn design of corbels and deep beams
4 .

Students will learn seismic design of reinforced concrete building frames and shear walls.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Students will be able to understand the basic seismology and characteristics of ground motions.
2. Students will be able to perform analysis of RC buildings under the earthquake and wind forces.
3. Students will be able to design beams, columns and determine the crack width of RC members.

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ID3205 : Interaction Design { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Foundations of Interaction Design:
This module introduces the core principles and scope of interaction design, exploring what constitutes good and poor design and how usability, accessibility, inclusiveness, and user experience goals shape interactive systems. Students will understand how user needs, behaviors, and goals influence design decisions. The process of interaction design, conceptual models, interaction types, paradigms, theories, and frameworks are also covered, providing a strong foundation for building user-centered interactive products.
Module 2 :

Cognitive, Social, and Emotional Aspects of Interaction:
Students explore how users think, perceive, and process information when interacting with systems. Cognitive models and frameworks are introduced to support user-centered design decisions. Social interaction concepts such as face-to-face vs. remote communication, co-presence, and collaboration are analyzed to inform system design. Emotional aspects — including affective design, persuasive technologies, and anthropomorphic interfaces — are discussed to enhance user engagement and satisfaction.
Module 3 :

Data-Driven Design: Gathering, Analysis, and Requirements:
This module focuses on the role of data in shaping interaction design. Students will learn various data-gathering techniques such as interviews, questionnaires, and observation, as well as how to choose and combine methods effectively. Quantitative and qualitative analysis techniques, visualization, and interpretation of findings are explored. The module also addresses ethical considerations in data handling and how data at scale can inform design. Techniques for discovering and capturing user requirements through personas, scenarios, and use cases are emphasized.
Module 4 :

Interface Design, Prototyping, and Construction:
Students learn about various interface types, including graphical, tangible, and natural user interfaces, and explore emerging interaction paradigms. The module emphasizes conceptual and concrete design, guiding students through the prototyping process using appropriate tools and methods. It also covers the construction of interactive systems, ensuring that prototypes balance usability, functionality, and emotional engagement while reflecting user needs and behaviors.
Module 5 :

Evaluation and Interaction Design in Practice:
The final module focuses on evaluating interactive systems and applying interaction design principles in real-world contexts. Students will study the purpose, timing, and methods of evaluation, including usability testing, field studies, heuristic evaluation, walkthroughs, analytics, A/B testing, and predictive models. Practical design approaches such as AgileUX, design patterns, and open-source resources are introduced, enabling students to create, iterate, and refine interactive solutions that meet user requirements and industry standards.

Course Objective

1 .

Understand the foundational principles of interaction design, usability, accessibility, and inclusiveness.
2 .

Apply user-centered design processes and integrate cognitive, social, and emotional aspects into interactive systems.
3 .

Employ data-gathering and analysis techniques to inform requirements and guide design decisions.
4 .

Design and prototype various types of interactive interfaces using appropriate tools and methods.
5 .

Evaluate interactive systems and apply interaction design practices such as AgileUX and design patterns to real-world solutions.

Course Outcome

1 .

Explain key principles of interaction design and user experience, and evaluate systems for usability and accessibility.
2 .

Apply cognitive, social, and emotional principles to create engaging user interactions.
3 .

Collect, analyze, and interpret user data to define requirements and guide design decisions.
4 .

Design and prototype effective interactive interfaces that address user needs and behaviors.
5 .

Conduct evaluations and implement real-world interaction design solutions using industry practices and tools.
